> Here are the 9 subdomains under `code`. What is missing? What is a distinction nobody in your field actually makes? What are we calling by the wrong name?

(03 §12.2, ask 1.) The family: Benchmarks whose scored artifact is software.

- Included: Tag this as PRIMARY if the entrant's task is to author software and the grader judges it by running, testing or verifying that software, or by scoring what the software computes, such as a trained model's predictions or an analysis result.
- Excluded: Do NOT tag this if code is the means to a result in another field, and do NOT tag it where the subject is operating a computer rather than authoring software: a grader that checks the end state of a machine the entrant operated makes it \`agents-tooluse\`, even where some tasks leave a program behind. An agentic harness does not move a benchmark out of this family; when tests judge a patch, this family is primary and \`agents-tooluse/software-agents\` is secondary (02 S12.11).

### 2.1 Aider polyglot benchmark (aider-polyglot)

`data/benchmarks/code/aider-polyglot.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*225 hard Exercism exercises in six languages, edited through aider and scored by their unit tests over two tries.*

The benchmark of aider, an open-source AI pair-programming tool, that its leaderboard uses to rank language models as code editors. It holds 225 Exercism practice exercises across six languages (C++ 26, Go 39, Java 47, JavaScript 49, Python 34, Rust 30), the hardest of the 697 Exercism offers in those languages: seven 2024 models each attempted all 697, and the benchmark keeps the problems that three or fewer of them solved. For each exercise the model is given Exercism's instructions and the stub source files, through aider, and must edit the files in an aider edit format (whole file, diff and others) so that aider can apply the changes. The exercise's own unit tests are then run in its language's toolchain inside a Docker container; if any fail, the model gets the test error output and a second try. The headline is the percentage of exercises whose tests all pass after the second try (pass\_rate\_2); the first-try rate, the percentage of responses in the correct edit format, cost and other statistics are published beside it. The exercises, with Exercism's example solutions, are public in the polyglot-benchmark repository, and the harness is in the aider repository. Results are added to the leaderboard's data file by pull request. It replaced aider's original code editing benchmark, all 133 Exercism Python exercises, which had saturated above 80%; the polyglot board's top score is 88.0% (gpt-5, high reasoning effort).

#### aider-polyglot · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/function-synthesis · [S4][aider-polyglot-s4]
  - why: Each exercise asks for an implementation of the stub functions or classes in one exercise's source files from a natural-language specification (Exercism's instructions), judged by running the exercise's unit tests, which is the leaf's definition. The edit-format requirement and the second try do not change what is scored.
  > This benchmark evaluates how effectively aider and LLMs can translate a natural language coding request into executable code saved into files that pass unit tests.
- `capability` = instruction-following · [S7][aider-polyglot-s7]
  - why: The leaderboard claims to measure following instructions as well as editing code, and it scores compliance with the edit format specified in the system prompt separately from correctness ("Correct edit format" beside "Percent correct"), which the term's inclusion test asks.
  > Measures the percent of coding tasks where the LLM complied with the edit format specified in the system prompt.
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests · [S4][aider-polyglot-s4]
  - why: The exercise's unit tests are run in its language's toolchain (pytest, cargo test, go test, npm, a C++ script, Gradle), and an exercise counts as solved when all of them pass.
  > which report the percent of the tasks which had all tests passing
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness · [S4][aider-polyglot-s4]
  - why: Every model is run through aider and the benchmark's own driver, which sends the instructions, applies the edits, runs the tests and returns their errors for one more try; a row names the model, its edit format and the aider command. The README calls it an end-to-end evaluation of aider and the LLM together.
  > It provides an end-to-end evaluation of not just the LLM's coding ability, but also its capacity to \*edit existing code\* and \*format those code edits\* so that aider can save the edits to the local source files.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `code/competitive-programming` · [S5][aider-polyglot-s5]
  - why: The exercises were selected for difficulty, but they are practice exercises without a contest's efficiency limits; the harness only stops a test run after three minutes.
  > timeout = 60 \* 3
- `domain` not `code/repository-scale-se` · [S6][aider-polyglot-s6]
  - why: The files to change are given and small (an exercise's stubs); there is no repository to search and no localisation step. A 2026 paper describes the tasks as single-file editing.
  > Its six programming languages and single-file editing objectives, evaluated by unit tests, define a task family that is distinct from the environments used for training.
- `capability` not `self-correction` · [S5][aider-polyglot-s5]
  - why: The second try is driven by the test error output, an external oracle telling the model what is wrong, which the term's exclusion test rules out, although the first-try and second-try rates are both published.
  > instructions += prompts.test\_failures.format(file\_list=file\_list)
- `designed_for_subjects` not `instruction-tuned-model` · [S7][aider-polyglot-s7]
  - why: The model is not prompted once; the harness returns test errors for a second try, and aider itself asks for a fixed copy of an edit it could not apply.
  > If the LLM makes edit mistakes, aider will give it feedback and ask for a fixed copy of the edit.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `agent-scaffold` · [S8][aider-polyglot-s8]
  - why: Entrants do not bring their own loop. Some rows pair two models in aider's architect mode (a planner and an editor model), but that is one of aider's own modes, chosen like an edit format, not an entrant's scaffold.
  > model: DeepSeek R1 + claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 edit\_format: architect
- `designed_for_subjects` not `reasoning-model` · [S8][aider-polyglot-s8]
  - why: Rows record reasoning-effort and thinking-token settings, but the benchmark is not built around a reasoning budget; they are run conditions (comparability).
  > test\_cases: 225 model: gpt-5 (high) edit\_format: diff commit\_hash: 32faf82 reasoning\_effort: high pass\_rate\_1: 52.0 pass\_rate\_2: 88.0

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type is null. Both repositories are in the Aider-AI organisation account, but the site's pages carry one person's byline and the harness writing is first-person. If Aider-AI is one person's organisation, individual (key-person risk) fits better than any organisational term; if it is a company, industry-lab. · [S14][aider-polyglot-s14]
   > "type":"Organization"
2. (field `capability`) capability instruction-following rests on the separately reported edit-format compliance and the leaderboard's own claim. The headline is test correctness, so a reviewer may prefer an empty capability, as HumanEval and BigCodeBench have. · [S2][aider-polyglot-s2]
   > ability to follow instructions and edit code successfully without human intervention
3. (field `lineage`) Lineage. The polyglot benchmark is modelled as its own benchmark that replaced the original 133-exercise Python code editing benchmark, not as a later edition of one aider family. Both are the same maintainer's, with the same task and protocol, so 04 S4's edition row is arguable; the old board is still published. Neither the old benchmark nor the refactoring benchmark has an id. · [S15][aider-polyglot-s15]
   > code editing benchmark asks the LLM to edit python source files to complete 133 small coding exercises from Exercism.
4. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The supporting evidence is the maintainer's 2023 supposition about the Python predecessor and the public example solutions; neither shows items in a model's training data, so high is not supported. No decontamination check exists. · [S13][aider-polyglot-s13]
   > It only sees the error output from failed tests. Of course, all of this code was probably part of its original training data!
5. (field `governance.submission_process`) submission\_process is self-reported plus maintainer-run. Merging a pull request may amount to a review, which would make it maintainer-verified, but no source states a check; no source says which rows the maintainer ran. · [S4][aider-polyglot-s4]
   > Submit results by opening a PR with edits to the
6. (field `activity`) activity accepting-submissions rests on the Contributing results page. The newest rows are from 2025-10-03, so whether pull requests are still merged is unconfirmed; closed may be the truer state. · [S8][aider-polyglot-s8]
   > command: aider --model deepseek/deepseek-chat date: 2025-10-03
7. (field `data.data_provenance`) The exercise selection used seven 2024 models' results (those solved by three or fewer were kept), so the set is adversarially filtered against those models, and a model family among them may be disadvantaged against later ones. No source discusses this bias. · [S3][aider-polyglot-s3]
   > each attempted all 697 of the Exercism problems
8. (field `designed_for_subjects`) designed\_for\_subjects model-in-benchmark-harness. The harness is aider itself, the maintainer's product, and scores move with the edit format and aider version; (execution-tests, model-in-benchmark-harness) resolves to the fallback comparability profile, so the material\_extra list carries the harness conditions.
9. (field `lineage`) The refactoring benchmark (89 large Python methods) is not recorded as lineage of this entry. It is the same maintainer's, with its own leaderboard, but a different task; if it is curated it needs its own id. · [S16][aider-polyglot-s16]
   > refactoring benchmark asks the LLM to refactor 89 large methods from large python classes.
10. (field `external_ids`) Epoch's string maps here with version null, and its score column "Percent correct" is presumably the leaderboard's pass\_rate\_2 (two tries); that should be confirmed before Epoch's rows are compared with first-try or pass@k numbers from papers. · [S17][aider-polyglot-s17]
   > Administered by the benchmark creator Aider Polyglot, APEX-Agents
11. (field `governance.independence_flags`) independence\_assessed is false. The maintainer's tool is the harness, not an entrant, and no funding statement was found; a reviewer with the site's sponsorship or company details could assess it.
12. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence is null. The repository has no licence file and defers to Exercism's track licences, which were not read. · [S11][aider-polyglot-s11]
   > "license":null

### 2.2 SWE-bench (swe-bench)

`data/benchmarks/code/swe-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence None · added 2026-09-23 · last verified 2026-11-18

*2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 Python repos; a system must patch the repo so the issue's tests pass.*

Each task instance pairs a GitHub issue with the repository at the commit its fixing pull request was based on. The system under test edits the codebase; the edit is applied as a patch and scored by running the tests the real pull request changed from failing to passing, together with tests that passed before and must still pass. The metric is the percentage of instances resolved.

### 2.3 SWE-Bench Pro (swe-bench-pro)

`data/benchmarks/code/swe-bench-pro.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Long-horizon tasks from copyleft and purchased startup repositories; an agent's patch must pass hidden tests.*

Scale AI's successor in design to SWE-bench: 1,865 tasks from 41 actively maintained repositories (business applications, B2B services, developer tools) in Python, Go, JavaScript and TypeScript. Each task pairs a repository at a base commit, in a Docker image built by professional engineers, with a human-rewritten problem statement, a list of requirements and, where needed, the interface the tests expect; the system must write a patch, which counts as resolved only if the task's fail-to-pass tests now pass and its pass-to-pass tests still do. Trivial edits are excluded; reference solutions average 107.4 lines across 4.1 files. The tasks are split three ways. The public set, from 11 GPL-style copyleft repositories, is released openly; the held-out set, from 12 other copyleft repositories, is kept private to check for overfitting; the commercial set, from 18 startups' proprietary repositories bought for the purpose, is kept private and scored by Scale, which publishes those results separately. The copyleft licences and the private codebases are the design's defence against contamination. V2 (September 2026, with Reflection AI) revised the public set to 642 tasks with a 51-task Hard split and a locked protocol (agent offline but for the model endpoint, every patch re-graded in a clean container) after agents were found retrieving upstream fixes and forging dependencies. The paper ran every model in the SWE-Agent scaffold; the V2 board reports each system as model, scaffold and effort.

#### swe-bench-pro · Domain and capabilities

- `domain.primary` = code/repository-scale-se · [S1][swe-bench-pro-s1]
  - why: The system gets a whole repository at a base commit and a task description, finds where to change it and writes a patch, typically across several files, which the task's tests judge. That is the leaf's definition, and the code family's exclusion test keeps a benchmark here when tests judge a patch, however agentic the harness.
  > The model must generate a patch file to resolve the issue and pass a suite of human-reviewed tests as validation.
- `domain.secondary` = agents-tooluse/software-agents, code/bug-repair · [S1][swe-bench-pro-s1]
  - why: software-agents because the protocol itself is agentic, unlike SWE-bench's paper protocol -- the paper runs every model in the SWE-Agent scaffold for up to 50 turns, and V2's locked protocol runs agents in a sandbox -- but tests judge the patch, so it is secondary (02 S12.11). bug-repair because the tasks include bug fixes beside feature requests, optimisations and refactoring; no source gives the share.
  > We include a diverse selection of feature requests as well as bug fixes
- `capability` = context-integration · [S1][swe-bench-pro-s1]
  - why: Each task supplies the requirements and interface that the hidden tests check, and the paper's ablation shows resolve rates falling steeply without them, so the supplied material determines success.
  > Without the requirements and interface, both models tested (GPT-5 and CLAUDE OPUS 4.1) show significantly degraded performance.
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests · [S1][swe-bench-pro-s1]
  - why: The patch is applied in the task's container and its fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests are run; the resolve rate is the headline.
  > Every task includes human-reviewed test suites with fail2pass tests that verify issue resolution and pass2pass tests that ensure existing functionalities remain intact.
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness, agent-scaffold · [S4][swe-bench-pro-s4]
  - why: The paper runs every model in one scaffold (SWE-Agent, its default prompt, 50 turns), so only the model varies, which is model-in-benchmark-harness. The V2 paper and board report each result as a system -- model, scaffold and reasoning effort, with Claude Code, Codex and mini-swe-agent -- which is agent-scaffold.
  > Because results depend on the scaffold and effort setting as well as the model, we report them per system, defined as the combination of the three.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `code/function-synthesis` · [S1][swe-bench-pro-s1]
  - why: No task is a self-contained function; every task is a change inside a repository whose location the system must find, and trivial edits were excluded.
  > To ensure task complexity, we exclude trivial edits (1–10 lines of code) and retain only problems requiring substantial, multi-file modifications.

### 2.4 ALE-Bench (ale-bench)

`data/benchmarks/code/ale-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*40 AtCoder Heuristic Contest optimisation problems; programs are scored and ranked against the contest's human field.*

Sakana AI's benchmark of algorithm engineering, built with AtCoder from 40 past AtCoder Heuristic Contest (AHC) problems held from March 2021 to April 2025: hard optimisation tasks such as routing, scheduling, packing and planning whose true optima are out of reach, so a solution is never right or wrong, only better or worse. Each problem ships with its statement (English and Japanese), a Rust scorer, the contest's input generator and visualisers, and the original contest's ranking data. The entrant writes a program (C++, Python or Rust in the mandated AtCoder 202301 judge environment) inside a timed session that mirrors the contest's length, about four hours for a short contest and one to two weeks for a long one; it may run test cases and visualise behaviour as often as it likes, and then submits once. The submission is run under the contest's execution limits on the original private test cases, its total score is placed in the contest's final human ranking, and the rank is converted into AtCoder's Elo-like performance. The headline is the average performance over the problems, with the share of problems above performance thresholds and an AtCoder rating beside it. A lite set of 10 problems is scored against rankings rebuilt on fewer private cases. The paper ran 22 models one-shot, four with four hours of self-refinement and two scaffolds; Sakana's own ALE-Agent reached the best lite result. The maintainers' live leaderboard (updated 2026-11-02) runs 151 models with its own sampling and self-refinement harness on the full set.

**Evidence** (44 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### ale-bench · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][ale-bench-s1]
  > We introduce ALE-Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating AI systems on score-based algorithmic programming contests.
- `released` = 2025-06-10 · [S1][ale-bench-s1]
  > Submitted on 10 Jun 2025 (v1), last revised 6 Oct 2025 (this version, v2)
- `release_venue` = NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  > 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.

#### ale-bench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/competitive-programming; secondary agents-tooluse/long-horizon-autonomy · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: The entrant writes a program, and the grader runs it on the contest's private test cases and scores what it computes, the code family's case. The problems are AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems kept under their original execution limits (2 to 10 seconds per case on a replica of AtCoder's environment) and ranked against the contest's own field, and the paper calls ALE-Bench a competitive programming benchmark. Each attempt is one unattended session as long as the original contest, with repeated test runs, which the secondary leaf records.
  > Just as previous competitive programming benchmarks have served as leading indicators of LLM reasoning capabilities, ALE-Bench, a more challenging competitive programming benchmark, can fulfill a similar function.
- `capability` = optimization · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: Every problem states an objective, its score function to be maximised or minimised over the test cases, and systems are ranked by how well their program optimises it; no exact solution is known, so the score keeps rising with better optimisation.
  > This benchmark is open-ended, in the sense that true optima are out of reach and scores can keep rising.
- `capability` = autonomy · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: The regulations forbid any human intervention once the run has started, apart from restarts after technical failures, and score what the unattended session submits.
  > No human intervention or assistance is permitted after the agent has received the problem statement and commenced its run.
- `evaluation_method` = human-distribution-percentile, execution-tests · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: The submitted program is compiled and run on the contest's private test cases under its time and memory limits, and each run's verdict (accepted, wrong answer, time limit exceeded) and score come from the problem's scorer. The total score is then ranked among the contest's actual human participants and turned into AtCoder's performance, so the headline locates the system in a measured human field.
  > Based on the overall private evaluation score, the agent is ranked relative to the original human participants of the contest.
- `designed_for_subjects` = agent-scaffold, model-in-benchmark-harness · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: The framework gives the entrant a session with test-run and visualisation actions and leaves the loop to it; the paper runs OpenHands and its own ALE-Agent. The paper's one-shot and self-refinement settings, and the leaderboard's repeated sampling with self-refinement, run every model through the maintainers' own loop, of which only the model varies.
  > ALE-Bench covers evaluation from bare LLMs to scaffolded agents.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `code/code-performance-optimization` · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: That leaf scores making given code faster with its behaviour preserved, on speedup. Here no code is given, the execution limit is a fixed constraint each program must meet, and the score is the problem's own objective (route length, packing quality) for the output the program computes, not its run time.
  > The tasks are typically CPU-bound, with execution time limits ranging from 2 to 10 seconds per case.
- `capability` not `self-correction` · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: Refinement is driven by the scorer's results on public test cases, an external oracle the term's exclusion test rules out, and only the final submission is scored.
  > success demands the ability to refine and improve solutions based on feedback
- `evaluation_method` not `entrant-relative-ranking` · [S3][ale-bench-s3]
  - why: The leaderboard also ranks models by their mean AI rank across problems, which moves when a model is added, but that is a secondary view; performance is computed against fixed human rankings.
  > With relative scoring, adding a new model can change the scores and rankings of existing entries.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `instruction-tuned-model` · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
  - why: Even the one-shot setting feeds compilation and format errors back for up to five generations, which is a loop the benchmark drives.
  > If scoring failed due to errors (e.g., compilation, formatting), feedback was provided, allowing up to five code generations.

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `domain`) Leaf: competitive-programming over code-performance-optimization. The deciding facts are that the problems are contest problems kept under their original execution limits and ranked against the contest's field (the paper calls ALE-Bench a competitive programming benchmark), and that the score is each problem's objective, with no given code to speed up and no speedup measured. But the leaf's definition speaks of correctness limits, and ALE-Bench is score-based with no correct answer, which the paper sets apart from the exact-solution contests the leaf was written for. Confirm, or open a heuristic-optimisation leaf. · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
   > Unlike those benchmarks, ALE-Bench tackles score-based tasks from the AtCoder Heuristic Contest (AHC) that have no single ground-truth answer.
2. (field `domain.secondary`) The secondary agents-tooluse/long-horizon-autonomy follows MLE-bench's reading of a long unattended session. The paper's one-shot setting and the leaderboard's sampled self-refinement have no long episode, and the paper cut every session to four hours, so the secondary describes the regulations rather than most reported results.
3. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method carries execution-tests beside human-distribution-percentile because the program is executed and judged per case (accepted, wrong answer, time limit), and the pair resolves the agentic profile. The score is an objective value rather than pass or fail, so human-distribution-percentile alone (the fallback profile, as MLE-bench has) is the alternative.
4. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) ceiling\_anchor\_type expert-average reads AtCoder's contestants as practising specialists; they are self-selected and range from novices to professionals, so crowd-average is arguable, and none-known fits the open-ended performance scale itself. · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
   > Human Average 1252 1257 1260 95.7 23.8 8.5 1414
5. (field `subsets`) Versions (04 S4): one revision, v1, with lite as a subset of the same release by the same maintainer. Lite is scored on fewer private cases against rankings rebuilt for it, so its performances are not comparable with full-set ones; a reviewer may prefer it as a variant or a track. Short and long formats are recorded as subsets because both the paper and the leaderboard report them separately. No concurrent line exists: the leaderboard's initial version (2025-06-17, archived on the site) and its current version are two states of one maintainer-run board, not two editions. · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
   > or a newly rebuilt laderboard with only the lite version subset of test cases (for the lite version)
6. (field `data.refresh`) refresh static and versions frozen rest on the dataset's lastModified of 2025-06-17 and the leaderboard's unchanged 40 problems. What changed on Hugging Face a week after the paper was not read; the toolkit's v1.5.0 changed the relative-score calculation and v1.4.0 added judge 202510 (GitHub releases API, not a quoted Source). If either changes what a performance means, versioned-releases applies. · [S6][ale-bench-s6]
   > "lastModified":"2025-06-17T05:58:33.000Z"
7. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. Every problem predates every leaderboard model's cutoff, and the paper's null result covers four models and a date-versus-cutoff plot, not a memorisation test; the private seeds and rankings reach the entrant's machine and are hidden only by the rules. High would need an evidenced route, which no source gives. · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
   > To investigate potential training data contamination, we analyzed performance variations based on contest dates
8. (field `activity`) activity no-submission-channel and submission\_process maintainer-run rest on finding no submission route in the README or on the leaderboard page; the repository's issues and contributing guide were not read, and an outside request route there would make it accepting-submissions.
9. (field `governance.maintainer`) Governance: maintainer\_type industry-lab names Sakana AI, which holds the repository, dataset and board, with AtCoder as co-developer; the README disclaims it as an official product of either company. The maintainer-competes flag rests on ALE-Agent in the paper only, not on the leaderboard. · [S7][ale-bench-s7]
   > This repository is not an official product of SakanaAI or AtCoder and is therefore not officially supported.
10. (field `ground_truth_source`) ground\_truth\_source repository-tests stands for the shipped scorers, private seeds and contest rankings; no enum value names an objective scorer with a human ranking. compute\_tier api-credits-only although the regulations fix the scoring CPU (Xeon 8375C or equivalent; the README recommends c6i.32xlarge, 128 vCPUs), which ordinary CPU may not meet.
11. (field `lineage`) Epoch's one string maps to this entry with version and subset null, and its export gives no score column or data file, so which set and protocol Epoch would use is unknown. The paper's protocols (one-shot with up to five retries; four hours of self-refinement; scaffolds) and the leaderboard's (15 samples, median kept, 1 to 16 self-refine steps) give non-comparable numbers. Not read: the derivatives an arXiv search shows, ALE-CLI (arXiv 2610.00917) and FrontierSmith's training use (arXiv 2605.14445), which may need lineage forks. · [S9][ale-bench-s9]
   > ALE-Bench,False,,,1.0,0.0,1.0,2025-06-10,
12. (field `data.access`) Personal data: the dataset's ranking.csv lists 6,139 AtCoder users' ranks and ratings, and the problem packages hold the contests' rankings and individual scores, which the regulations forbid entrants to read; neither was downloaded, and AtCoder's contest and ranking pages were not fetched. Whether the entry should flag the dataset as holding personal data is for the reviewer. · [S2][ale-bench-s2]
   > This leaderboard lists the ranks and ratings of 6,139 active users

**Reviewer checklist** for `ale-bench`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.5 CRUXEval (cruxeval)

`data/benchmarks/code/cruxeval.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*800 short Python functions: predict an output (CRUXEval-O) or an input (CRUXEval-I), checked by execution.*

800 short Python functions (3 to 13 lines), each paired with an input and the output that executing the function on that input produces. The functions and inputs were generated by Code Llama 34B from prompts naming Python standard-library str, dict and list methods, then filtered to short, deterministic programs without imports, floating point or large arithmetic, which the authors judge a good programmer could trace in about a minute. Two tasks are scored separately: CRUXEval-O gives the function and the input and asks for the output; CRUXEval-I gives the function and the output and asks for any input that produces it. A prediction is checked by executing the assertion f(input) == output with the prediction in place, and results are pass@1 (temperature 0.2) and pass@5 (temperature 0.8) over sampled generations. The paper prompts base models few-shot and GPT models zero-shot, with and without chain of thought. The maintainers' leaderboard lists 43 runs, from Phi-1 to GPT-4o and Claude 3 Opus. Derived benchmarks, such as the multilingual CRUXEval-X, are separate entries.

#### cruxeval · Identity and id

  > CRUXEval-X extends CRUXEval to a multilingual setting

#### cruxeval · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/code-understanding · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
  - why: Every item asks a question about a given program's execution, its output on an input or an input for an output, and nothing is written or changed in the program; the paper names both tasks as measures of code understanding and execution.
  > \1) output prediction, CRUXEval-O to measure code execution following and 2) input prediction, CRUXEval-I to measure code reasoning and understanding
- `capability` = deductive-reasoning · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
  - why: Each answer is fixed by the function and the given input or output alone, since executing the function deterministically produces the stored output, and the benchmark was filtered so that tracing it needs no arithmetic beyond small operands.
  > CRUXEval consists of 800 distinct functions, each with an input-output pair such that executing the function on the input deterministically produces the output.
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
  - why: A prediction is placed in the item's assertion, which is executed; it counts only if the assertion passes.
  > For input prediction, a generated input passes if assert f(generated input) == output passes, and for output prediction, a generated output passes if assert f(input) == generated output passes.
- `designed_for_subjects` = base-model, instruction-tuned-model · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
  - why: The paper's direct prompts end in an open assertion for raw continuation, with two worked examples for every model except the GPT models, which are given an instruction zero-shot; base models (Code Llama, StarCoder, DeepSeek Coder base) and instruction-tuned ones are evaluated side by side.
  > We use a few-shot prompt for all models other than GPT models.

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `quantitative-reasoning` · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
  - why: The filters remove floating point, true division and large integer operations, so the path to an answer is program tracing, not calculation.
  > we ensure the samples in our benchmark are simple (maximum 13 lines, no complex arithmetic)
- `capability` not `tool-use` · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
  - why: The protocol gives the model no tools. The paper notes that an interpreter would solve output prediction outright, which is why tools\_allowed is material (comparability).
  > one might object that output prediction can simply be done with a Python interpreter

Generations that do not follow the format count as wrong. · [S1][cruxeval-s1]

**Open review checks** (7):

1. (field `domain`) Domain: code/code-understanding fits the leaf definition, but the code family's inclusion test speaks of authoring software judged by running it. Here the entrant writes only an input expression or an output literal that an executed assertion judges. If that is not authoring software, the family test and the leaf disagree.
2. (field `capability`) deductive-reasoning rests on each answer being fixed by the program and its input or output. The premises include Python's library semantics, which the item does not state, and CRUXEval-I is an inverse search; a reviewer may prefer an empty capability, as HumanEval has.
3. (field `evaluation_method`) execution-tests over exact-match. For CRUXEval-O the executed assertion amounts to value equality with the stored output; the call rests on CRUXEval-I accepting any input and on equality being Python's, not a string comparison. · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
   > For input prediction, a generated input passes if assert f(generated input) == output passes, and for output prediction, a generated output passes if assert f(input) == generated output passes.
4. (field `activity`) activity no-submission-channel. The two SemCoder rows "(under verification)" suggest results arrived from outside the maintainers at least once; if that was a route, it is now shut (the repository is archived) and closed would fit instead. · [S9][cruxeval-s9]
   > semcoder-6.7b+cot (under verification), 62.5,81.4,64.4,79.1
5. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on Meta's Code Llama runs on Meta's leaderboard, which the maintainers ran as baselines, and on Code Llama 34B having generated the items; the paper's test found no own-data advantage. · [S1][cruxeval-s1]
   > evaluating a model on its own generated data does not seem to provide it a significant advantage
6. (field `aggregation_policy`) aggregation\_policy unknown because the two tasks are never combined; none-by-design would need the maintainers to say so, and they do not.
7. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) measured-ceiling rests on every stored output having come from executing its function, which makes each reference answer pass; no source reports running the scorer on the reference answers.

### 2.6 DafnyBench (dafnybench)

`data/benchmarks/code/dafnybench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*782 Dafny programs with their assertions and invariants removed; restore hints so Dafny proves the unchanged spec.*

782 stand-alone Dafny programs, each in a ground\_truth version that Dafny 4.3.0 verifies and a hints\_removed version with every assert and loop-invariant statement deleted from the method bodies, without marking where. The model is given the hints\_removed program and must return the whole program with hints filled back in. An attempt succeeds if Dafny verifies the result, every requires and ensures clause is kept, and neither {:verify false} nor assume false is used. The paper's protocol gives each model up to 10 attempts at temperature 0.3, feeding back Dafny's error message after each failure, and reports the success rate over all programs. 556 programs come from a deduplicated scrape of public Dafny files on GitHub from before the end of 2023, 62 from the Clover benchmark and 164 from dafny-synthesis, whose programs are GPT-4 translations of MBPP problems. Dafny alone verifies 26.9% of the programs with no hints added; Claude 3 Opus, the best of five models in the paper, reaches about 68%. Later work reports far higher rates with its own scaffolds, and one 2026 paper repairs 70 base programs that do not compile.

#### dafnybench · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][dafnybench-s1]

- `release_venue` = The 4th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI at NeurIPS 2024 · [S2][dafnybench-s2]

#### dafnybench · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/program-verification · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
  - why: Each item asks for the annotations that let a program verifier prove a program's own specification (its methods' requires and ensures clauses), so what is proved is a property of the program, which the leaf's note against mathematics/formal-theorem-proving makes decisive.
  > asked LLM to fill hints back in so that the resulting program could be verified with Dafny
- `capability` = deductive-reasoning · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
  - why: Whether an answer counts is decided by the verifier deriving the unchanged postconditions from the program, its preconditions and the inserted hints, with nothing outside the item consulted.
  > \1) The reconstructed program is verified with Dafny; 2) LLM preserves all preconditions (requires statements) and postconditions (ensures statements)
- `evaluation_method` = formal-proof-check · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
  - why: The Dafny verifier, an SMT-backed program verifier, accepts or rejects the reconstructed program, and the check that the requires and ensures clauses were kept and no verification was switched off is part of the same verdict, as the term's inclusion test allows.
  > \1) The reconstructed program is verified with Dafny; 2) LLM preserves all preconditions (requires statements) and postconditions (ensures statements)
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
  - why: The benchmark's own scripts drive every model through the same loop of up to ten attempts, returning Dafny's error message after each failure, with near-identical prompts (adjusted per model family) and fixed hyperparameters, so only the model varies between the paper's rows.
  > If the model failed on any of the intermediate attempts, it received the Dafny error message and was asked to filled in the hints again with the error message taken into consideration.

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `self-correction` · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
  - why: The protocol retries with Dafny's error message, but that is an external oracle saying what is wrong, which the term's exclusion test names, and only success within ten attempts is scored.
  > If the model failed on any of the intermediate attempts, it received the Dafny error message and was asked to filled in the hints again with the error message taken into consideration.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `classical-algorithm` · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
  - why: Dafny run on the hints\_removed programs is a no-LLM baseline that sets the floor (26.9%), not a designed-for entrant.
  > Dafny succeeds in auto-verifying some programs even without hints

1. (field `id`) Choice among the candidates for code/program-verification: DafnyBench was taken for the most 2025-2026 use (an arXiv search on 2026-11-09 found nine later papers naming it in their abstracts, five of them in 2026), open ungated Apache-2.0 data and a full harness. Its repository has not been pushed since 2024-12-12, while CLEVER's (trishullab/clever) was pushed on 2026-08-26; FVAPPS's was last pushed in May 2025. Verus-Bench and VerifyThisBench were not looked up. If maintenance should outweigh use, CLEVER is the alternative.
2. (field `id`) The id dafnybench is proposed, not allocated (04 S3); no Epoch stub exists.
3. (field `domain`) Domain: program-verification holds for the items as a whole, but the scraped programs carry lemmas (1.40 per program on average) and the paper does not say how many state mathematical rather than program facts; if many do, mathematics/formal-theorem-proving is a secondary.
4. (field `lineage`) lineage role fork, by the MMLU-Pro precedent (grew out of earlier benchmarks and subsumes them), although 556 of 782 programs are new; root is arguable. No link targets exist, as Clover, dafny-synthesis and MBPP have no entries. · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
   > we cite the existing verifiable programming benchmarks that we subsume in DafnyBench
5. (field `data.size`) The constituents' counts do not match the paper's own description of them, 62 programs taken from a Clover of 66 and 164 from a dafny-synthesis of 153; no source explains either difference. · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
   > dafny-synthesis translates 153 MBPP problems from Python to Dafny using GPT-4
6. (field `data.ceiling_anchor_type`) measured-ceiling rests on every ground\_truth program verifying with Dafny 4.3.0. DafnyPro reports that 70 hints\_removed programs do not compile, which the released version still contains; whether all 782 remain solvable from their hints\_removed form, and under later Dafny versions, is untested in any source. · [S2][dafnybench-s2]
   > several base programs in the existing DafnyBench dataset are not compilable
7. (field `versions`) DafnyPro's repair of 70 base programs is a third party's corrected copy, not a maintainer revision, so no version is recorded; if the repaired copy is published and adopted, it is a fork with its own entry.
8. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination medium. The scored programs predate every current model's cutoff and the hinted solutions are public beside them, which makes high arguable, but no source evidences a model trained on them. · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
   > To mitigate data contamination, models run on our benchmark should ideally not be trained on data from the repositories listed in Appendix D.
9. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence Apache-2.0 follows the Hugging Face tag and GitHub's metadata; the paper names Apache 2.0 and the GPL v3.0 together, and the scraped files keep their own licences, some with none. · [S3][dafnybench-s3]
   > we release our derivative DafnyBench repository under an Apache 2.0 license and a GNU General Public License v3.0
10. (field `release_venue`) release\_venue comes from DafnyPro's reference list (a NeurIPS 2024 workshop); the DafnyBench paper and README do not name a venue, and the workshop's own page was not read.
11. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type individual: the repository and dataset sit in personal accounts, although the paper's authors are an academic collaboration. ### 2.7 MLE-bench (mle-bench)

`data/benchmarks/code/mle-bench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*75 Kaggle competitions run offline by an AI agent, scored by the Kaggle medal its submission would have won.*

OpenAI's benchmark of machine-learning engineering by AI agents: 75 finished Kaggle competitions, chosen by hand from 586 candidates, each with its description, its data and grading code, run offline in a container. The agent must train a model and write a submission.csv of test-set predictions; writing predictions by hand, calling another language model and copying public solutions are forbidden, and a log-analysis tool and a plagiarism detector check for them. Where Kaggle never released test labels, the maintainers split the public training data anew. Each submission is graded with its competition's metric and placed on a snapshot of the competition's Kaggle private leaderboard, so it earns the bronze, silver or gold medal it would have won there; the headline is the percentage of attempts that win any medal, the mean over at least three seeds. Competitions are labelled Low (22), Medium (38) or High (15) complexity, and the Low split doubles as MLE-bench Lite. The canonical setup gives an agent 24 hours per competition on a machine with one A10 GPU, which the README recommends rather than requires. The README's leaderboard ranks agent scaffolds paired with models; it stopped taking submissions on 2026-04-24, and fixes for known task defects are held back for a v2.

- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.8 DABstep (dabstep)

`data/benchmarks/code/dabstep.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*450 data-analysis questions over one payments dataset and its manual, each scored on one hidden factoid answer.*

Adyen and Hugging Face's benchmark of data-analysis agents, launched with a live leaderboard in February 2025 and described in a June 2025 paper. Its 450 questions are drawn from analysts' work at Adyen, anonymised and expanded from 95 core questions by varying merchants, dates and thresholds. Every question is answered from the same seven context files: a payments table of about 138,000 transactions, merchant and fee tables in CSV and JSON, and Markdown documentation, including a manual of fee rules. The launch post says the data were generated synthetically. 72 questions are Easy, mostly one table, and 378 are Hard, needing several files, the manual and multi-step code; each comes with guidance fixing the answer's format. A system's final answer (a number, a short string or a list) is scored by quasi exact match, with a numeric tolerance, order-free lists and fuzzy string matching. The 450 questions are published without answers and a 10-question dev set with them; the Space scores uploaded answer files against a private copy of the keys and reports Easy and Hard accuracy, ranked on Hard. DABstep prescribes no agent loop, and rows name an agent and its model. The board has a Validated tab, for top-10 entries checked by the maintainers, and an Unvalidated one. The maintainers stopped validating on 2026-07-22, announcing a v2. The unvalidated tab still takes entries, and 15 of its rows score 100% on both levels. The per-task results of every submission, answers included, are public in the same dataset.

#### dabstep · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/data-science-workflows; secondary society-econ-law/financial-analysis · [S1][dabstep-s1]
  - why: The entrant writes and runs code over the supplied data files to compute each answer, and the grader scores what that analysis computes, the code family's "analysis result" case, and the data-science-workflows leaf's analysis reaching a quantitative answer. The questions are payments analysis (fees, fraud rates, merchant costs), which the secondary leaf records. It is not primary, since the claim is data analysis by agents, the domain knowledge needed is supplied in the manual, and the launch post calls the data synthetic, which society-econ-law's exclusion of a general competence using economic content as material covers.
  > requiring models to combine code-based data processing with contextual reasoning over heterogeneous documentation
- `capability` = quantitative-reasoning · [S4][dabstep-s4]
  - why: Most answers are numbers (fees, rates, counts, deltas) reached by filtering, aggregating and applying fee formulas, rounded as the guidance asks.
  > what is the total fees (in euros) that Belles\_cookbook\_store should pay?", "answer": "", "guidelines": "Answer must be just a number rounded to 2 decimals.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S3][dabstep-s3]
  - why: The answers depend on the supplied files, and the Hard questions on fee rules defined only in the benchmark's own manual, which an agent must read and apply.
  > demanding both technical data analysis skills (using code) and domain-specific understanding learned from the provided context
- `evaluation_method` = numeric-tolerance-match, exact-match · [S6][dabstep-s6]
  - why: Each question has one answer. The scorer lowercases and trims both strings; numbers are compared after stripping commas and currency signs, within a relative and absolute tolerance of 1e-4, or after rounding to the shorter of the two decimal expansions; lists are split on commas or semicolons, sorted and compared element by element; other strings must match once punctuation and spaces are removed, or one-word answers may be a subset of the other, or reach a similarity ratio above 0.95. Accuracy per level is the share of questions marked correct.
  > return math.isclose(num1, num2, rel\_tol=1e-4, abs\_tol=1e-4)
- `designed_for_subjects` = agent-scaffold · [S5][dabstep-s5]
  - why: DABstep supplies questions and files, not a loop; the entrant's agent decides what code to run and when to answer. Leaderboard rows give an agent name beside a model family, and the maintainers' ReAct baseline is offered for reproduction, not required.
  > Reproduce the baseline results with the agent code we open sourced

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `agents-tooluse/web-navigation` · [S3][dabstep-s3]
  - why: GAIA, which also scores one factoid answer per question on a Hugging Face board, is filed in agents-tooluse because its answers are found by operating the web. Here the answer is computed by code over supplied files, and the agents-tooluse exclusion sends an analysis the agent built to code. No agents-tooluse leaf fits as secondary either; tool-api-calling scores the calls themselves.
  > Especially in the Hard split (84% of tasks), no question can be answered through a single direct execution.
- `capability` not `autonomy` · [S5][dabstep-s5]
  - why: No source prohibits or measures human intervention; validation only confirmed that a top result came from an agent, and it has stopped.
  > confirms that a submission's results were achieved using a novel approach involving data analysis agents
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S3][dabstep-s3]
  - why: The paper chose factoid answers to avoid a judge model; the scorer is deterministic, and it agreed with two annotators on all 75 answers checked.
  > Our scoring function matched human judgment on all 75 examples, achieving 100% accuracy.
- `designed_for_subjects` not `model-in-benchmark-harness` · [S3][dabstep-s3]
  - why: The paper's baselines ran one standard ReAct wrapper (Hugging Face's smolagents, its reference 36) for every model, but submissions bring their own agents, and the board ranks them together with the baselines.
  > The entire setup consisted of a lightweight wrapper \[36\] around the LLM API

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on the maintainers' own baseline rows, ReAct and reasoning-prompt agents over third-party models in Hugging Face's smolagents library, not on a model of their own. The flag's definition (the maintainer submits systems evaluated by it) fits the rows literally; a reviewer may hold that baselines are not competing entries. · [S8][dabstep-s8]
   > \["\*\*Claude 4 Sonnet ReACT Baseline\*\*",81.94,19.84,"Hugging Face"
2. (field `domain`) Candidate choice for code/data-science-workflows. DABstep was chosen over DSBench (its data-analysis half is ModelOff spreadsheet questions graded in part by a GPT-4 judge, and its modelling half is Kaggle-style, closer to ml-engineering), DA-Code (it also scores computed outputs, and DS-STAR reports on it, but its own board was not checked here, and many of its outputs are charts and model predictions, nearer ml-engineering), DS-1000 (completions of StackOverflow snippets judged by tests, which is function-synthesis), and BLADE (it scores analysis decisions against expert ones, not a quantitative answer). DiscoveryBench was set aside as instructed. Its grader checks only the final answer, so the code exclusion ("code is the means to a result in another field") was weighed; the answer is what the agent's analysis computes, the inclusion test's own case, and the claim is data analysis, not finance. · [S1][dabstep-s1]
   > requiring models to combine code-based data processing with contextual reasoning over heterogeneous documentation
3. (field `data.data_provenance`) The leaf asks for an analysis "over real data". The paper calls the tasks real-world and the payments data anonymised transactions; the launch post's footnote says the data and the business context were generated synthetically. data\_provenance records the questions only. Which description holds, and how the data were generated, needs the maintainers. The missing term for data synthesised by an unstated method is logged as taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-09-dabstep-002. · [S2][dabstep-s2]
   > Tasks are realistic, the data has been generated synthetically.
4. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk is medium, lowered in review from the draft's high, because the leak routes are read from the files rather than stated by a source. The task\_scores split shows each submission's answer beside its verdict, so every answer marked true is a scored key in public (o4-mini's file alone marks 110 correct), and six dev answers are scored questions. 15 unvalidated rows score 100% on both levels, the first on 2025-12-12. High is the alternative if a reviewer takes the public keys as enough. · [S8][dabstep-s8]
   > \["\*\*openGauss Data Agent\*\*",100.0,100.0,"Agent of openGauss
5. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle under-revision rests on the 2026-07-22 notice of a v2 "in the coming weeks", which had not appeared by 2026-11-09. Whether v2 reissues these questions (under-revision) or adds a new set beside a finished v1, and whether it will be its own entry, is not known; active is the alternative if the v2 work has stopped. · [S5][dabstep-s5]

6. (field `lifecycle`) Saturation. The validated top is 89.95% Hard and 87.5% Easy (2026-02-22), below the 0.95 headroom line, while the open tab has rows at 100%. Which board measures headroom, and whether the unvalidated rows should count, needs a ruling; the launch post expected the benchmark to be solved in its current state. · [S2][dabstep-s2]
   > we foresee that the benchmark will eventually be considered solved in its current state
7. (field `data.refresh`) data.refresh is unset. The Space's commit list shows a commit fixing the evaluation and the scorer test on 2025-04-20, after launch, which would rule out static if it changed verdicts, and no version label marks it; the commit diff was not read.
8. (field `evaluation_method`) The paper's scorer description (Levenshtein, a 1e-2 tolerance in Algorithm 1) differs from the code, which also accepts a one-word answer that is a subset of the key or the reverse; exact-match is tagged beside numeric-tolerance-match although fuzzy and subset matching go beyond its whitespace-or-case normalisation (taxonomy/\_failures/2026-11-09-dabstep-001). · [S6][dabstep-s6]

9. (field `governance.submission_process`) submission\_process lists maintainer-verified for the Validated tab, which is now frozen, beside held-out-server for the open route. Whether a frozen validation record should still be tagged, or recorded in history only, is a modelling call.
10. (field `domain`) The secondary leaf society-econ-law/financial-analysis is defined over financial documents and statements; DABstep's material is payment transactions, fee tables and a processing manual. It may not fit, in which case no secondary applies.
11. (field `lineage`) Lineage. DS-STAR evaluates on DABStep-Research (the DABStep-Research paper, 2025), a report-generation suite whose name suggests it derives from DABstep; its maintainer and relation were not read, so no fork is recorded. The paper's own size statement ("the majority" of tasks hidden) also differs from the Space, which scores all 450. · [S7][dabstep-s7]

### 2.9 AlgoTune (algotune)

`data/benchmarks/code/algotune.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*154 numerical library functions; a model must make each faster while a verifier still accepts its outputs.*

A benchmark of code optimisation. Each of 154 tasks, in 13 categories from matrix operations and convex optimisation to graphs, signal processing, ODEs and cryptography, is a Python class with an input generator, a reference solver (usually a call into NumPy, SciPy, CVXPY, scikit-learn, NetworkX or OR-Tools) and a solution verifier. The entrant writes a faster solve function. On each task the submission is run on held-out test inputs sized so the reference takes about 100 ms on one CPU core; if the verifier accepts every output, the task score is the ratio of reference runtime to submission runtime (the minimum of ten timed runs), and an invalid or slower solution scores 1x. The AlgoTune score is the harmonic mean over all tasks, a metric with no upper bound. Tasks were contributed by 21 library committers and academics and each reviewed by two others. The maintainers also built AlgoTuner, a SWE-agent-like loop with a $1 budget per task, and the site's leaderboard ranks models run inside it (GPT-5.2 at 2.05x on 2026-11-09). The task count fell from 155 to 154 in the paper's second version, and since January 2026 the maintainers have tightened several verifiers against exploits, without version labels.

#### algotune · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/code-performance-optimization · [S1][algotune-s1]
  - why: The entrant writes code, the verifier runs it on test inputs and must accept every output, and the score is the speedup over the reference implementation, which is the leaf's definition (faster while preserving behaviour, scored on speedup rather than correctness alone).
  > We score an AI system based on how much faster its generated implementations are relative to our reference implementations.
- `capability` = optimization · [S1][algotune-s1]
  - why: The benchmark states its objective, runtime relative to the reference under a correctness gate, and ranks systems by how far they push it, with no bound on the score.
  > In AlgoTune, we score systems based on the speed of their synthesized code relative to a reference implementation, a metric with no absolute upper bound.
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests · [S1][algotune-s1]
  - why: The submitted code is executed on the test inputs, and only if the task's verifier accepts every output is a speedup assigned; an invalid solution scores the 1x floor.
  > If the task verifier deems all outputs valid, we assign the model a speedup score: the ratio between reference code runtime and LM code runtime over the test inputs.
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness, agent-scaffold · [S1][algotune-s1]
  - why: The paper and the leaderboard run every model inside the maintainers' AlgoTuner loop with the same commands and a $1 budget per task, and rows name only the model. The benchmark itself takes code from any system, and the README evaluates solver code placed in its results directory without the agent, which is how papers bring their own search harnesses (as\_used).
  > We evaluate all LMs with a fixed budget of $1 for each task.

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `creativity-novelty` · [S1][algotune-s1]
  - why: The paper hopes for algorithmic discovery and reports finding none, but scoring does not reward departure from known solutions; a faster call into another library scores the same as a new algorithm.
  > We did not observe AlgoTuner finding any novel algorithmic improvements across any of the LMs tested.
- `evaluation_method` not `constraint-check` · [S1][algotune-s1]
  - why: Each verifier asserts properties of an output (shape, orthonormality, an objective within tolerance), but the code must be run to produce the output and its runtime, which the term's exclusion test sends to execution-tests.
  > The solution verifier validates an LM-proposed solution for the given problem instance, returning a boolean value.

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `domain`) GSO, drafted for the same leaf by another agent, also scores runtime speedups on Python code. The paper describes it as optimising the runtime of functions inside popular Python repositories (NumPy, pandas, Pydantic), and sets AlgoTune apart as end-to-end algorithms across many domains. Each AlgoTune task is a self-contained class whose reference solver is a library call, scored as a harmonic mean of speedups over 154 such tasks, with no repository to work in. Both fit code-performance-optimization as primary, and gso.yaml adds repository-scale-se. The facets differ on purpose. GSO rejects optimization because its OPT@1 counts patches past 95% of a human speedup, while AlgoTune's score is the speedup itself, so optimization is tagged here. GSO logs its gap as a capability (gso-001, performance-engineering) and this entry as an evaluation method (algotune-001); the two records should be triaged together. · [S1][algotune-s1]
   > Our approach complements their work since we focus on implementing end-to-end algorithms from a wide variety of domains

### 2.10 GSO (gso)

`data/benchmarks/code/gso.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-09 · last verified 2026-11-09

*102 expert speedups from 10 open-source repositories; an agent must match each while keeping outputs unchanged.*

A benchmark of software performance optimization by coding agents, from UC Berkeley. An automated pipeline scanned the commit histories of popular GitHub repositories with an LLM judge for performance-improving commits, had an LLM write performance tests for each candidate that exercise a real workload and check the outputs before and after the commit for equivalence, and kept commits that made several tests markedly faster; a manual review then removed tasks with weak tests or ones that trivial tricks such as memoisation could pass. The result is 102 tasks from 10 codebases (NumPy 36, pandas 34, Pillow and Pillow-SIMD 11, the rest four or fewer each: Pydantic, Tornado, tokenizers, transformers, datasets, llama.cpp), about 60% of which need edits outside Python (C, C++, Cython, Rust, SIMD). The agent gets the repository at the commit before the expert's, its build commands and one performance test as the specification, and must return a patch. The patch is scored on all the task's performance tests: it must apply, keep every equivalence check passing and reach at least 95% of the expert commit's speedup, measured as the harmonic mean of per-test speedups (OPT@1, estimated from three rollouts in the paper). The maintainers run every model themselves inside the OpenHands scaffold and publish raw OPT@1 beside a hack-adjusted score, in which an LLM Hack Detector penalises deceptive optimizations such as memoisation or harness hijacking. Since release they have hardened the task environment against ground-truth leaks (stripping git refs to the expert commit, removing hidden test scripts from the Docker images, cutting containers off from GitHub after models were seen fetching upstream commits) and twice changed the elicitation. Top scores rose from under 5% in May 2025 to 88.2% in September 2026.

#### gso · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary code/code-performance-optimization; secondary code/repository-scale-se, agents-tooluse/software-agents · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: The entrant authors a patch and the grader runs it, checking equivalence and measuring runtime against the expert commit's; a correct patch that is not fast enough fails, which is the leaf's "scored on speedup rather than on correctness alone". The change is made inside a whole real repository, where finding the bottleneck is part of the task (repository-scale-se), by an agent that edits files, rebuilds and runs tests itself (software-agents, secondary because tests judge the patch).
  > SWE-Agents receive a performance test as task specification and must produce an optimization patch that improves runtime efficiency while maintaining correctness.
- `capability` = context-integration · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: The supplied repository and performance test decide what must change; the agent has to find the bottleneck in that codebase, and the expert edit averages over 100 lines across about four files.
  > Each task consists of an initial codebase snapshot, performance tests measuring runtime and correctness, a build script for environment setup, and a reference human commit establishing the target performance threshold.
- `evaluation_method` = execution-tests · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: The patch is applied and the task's performance tests run; success needs a clean apply, every equivalence assertion passing and a measured runtime at the threshold, all outcomes of executing the code.
  > Success requires that the patch (1) applies cleanly, (2) passes all correctness checks, and (3) matches or exceeds the target human commit
- `designed_for_subjects` = model-in-benchmark-harness, agent-scaffold · [S4][gso-s4]
  - why: The paper and the leaderboard run every model in one maintainer-chosen OpenHands configuration with GSO's own task prompt, so only the model varies. The harness itself scores a file of patches from any agent, and the maintainers have released integrations for other scaffolds, Harbor among them.
  > Scaffold: All models are run with the OpenHands scaffold unless otherwise specified.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `code/bug-repair` · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: The base code is correct; nothing is broken, and the specification is a performance test rather than an issue or a failing test.
  > performance tests natively provide precise specifications for correctness and efficiency
- `capability` not `optimization` · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: Runtime is the objective, but the score is not its value. OPT@1 is the share of tasks whose patch passes a fixed threshold, 95% of a human speedup, and the paper keeps raw speedups as a secondary metric.
  > we denote OPT@K as the OPT0.95@K metric that uses a 95% threshold for evaluating success against the human target
- `capability` not `long-horizon-execution` · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: An attempt runs for up to three hours over many steps, but a failed build or a slow patch can be reverted and retried within it, so an intermediate error does not make success unattainable, which the term's inclusion test asks.
  > we configure the agent with a 3-hour time limit per task and a 20-minute timeout per step
- `capability` not `tool-use` · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: The tools (a file editor and a bash terminal) are OpenHands'; the score is the patch's speedup, not whether tools were called correctly.
  > The scaffold provides access to a file-editor tool and a bash terminal tool to the agent
- `evaluation_method` not `domain-metric` · [S3][gso-s3]
  - why: Speedup, the harmonic mean of per-test runtime ratios, is a general measure from systems benchmarking, and it enters the score only as a pass/fail gate against the human commit.
  > we compute speedup using the harmonic mean of individual test speedups which is more robust to extreme positive outliers
- `evaluation_method` not `model-graded-judge` · [S4][gso-s4]
  - why: The Hack Detector is an LLM (GPT-5.4 at xhigh effort since 2026-04-27; the v0.1.9 harness defaults to GPT-5.6-Sol) that reads the patch against the oracle solution and tests, but it sets only the hack-adjusted column; the threshold curves use raw scores, and the leaderboard ranks by the raw score (its script, read but not quoted).
  > The "Hack-Adjusted" column shows scores after this penalty.
